propositions.text: Claimant alleges he is a Convention refugee due to imputed political opinion as a UDPS member.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the claimant), a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), is claiming that he is a "Convention refugee" pursuant to section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) because of his alleged imputed political opinion given that he is a member of the UDPS.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges he is a Convention refugee due to imputed political opinion as a UDPS member.

propositions.text: Claimant states he is a person in need of protection fearing arrest, detention, and torture by government and ANR due to opposition membership and protest participation.
propositions.quote: The claimant also states that he is "a person in need of protection" because he is afraid of being arrested, detained and tortured by the government of Joseph Kabila and the Agence Nationale de Renseignements (ANR) [national intelligence agency] because he is a member of the opposition and he participated in a few demonstrations.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant states he fears arrest and torture by government and ANR due to opposition membership and protests.

propositions.text: Claimant had a permanent job from 2005 to 2011 and was a UDPS member since 1994 with political problems in 2006, 2010, and 2011.
propositions.quote: He had a permanent job as a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX) from XXXX 2005 until he left the DRC in XXXX 2011. The claimant stated that he had problems because of his activism as a member of the UDPS, which he had been a member of since 1994. He had problems because of his political affiliations, among other things, in 2006, 2010 and 2011.

propositions.text: Claimant participated in a 2010 opposition march, was arrested, beaten, photographed, and released after two days without questioning.
propositions.quote: The claimant stated that, on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010 (amended to XXXX), he participated in a march organized by the various opposition parties demanding that the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The claimant was arrested along with XXXX other people. He was beaten during transportation to prison. When he was released from prison (amended to upon his arrival in prison) the authorities took his photograph. The claimant was released from prison without being questioned two days later.

propositions.text: In 2011, masked men attacked claimant's home; he escaped, wife was gang raped, and attackers stole valuables.
propositions.quote: On XXXX XXXX, 2011, masked men went to his house at 4:00 a.m., but luckily, he escaped out the window. His wife was gang raped. The attackers stole everything of value that he possessed.

propositions.text: Claimant received a photograph from a family friend's brother who works for XXXX, showing him when arrested (amended).
propositions.quote: On XXXX XXXX, 2011, at his sister's (amended to at his cousin's) home, a friend of his brother's who works for the XXXX gave him the photograph that had been taken when he was released (amended to arrested).

propositions.text: In 2011, employer recommended claimant take a course in Canada; claimant obtained false letter and Canadian visitor visa, arriving in 2011 and attending course for two weeks.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2011, his employer recommended that he take a course in Canada. Through his NGO contacts, the claimant obtained a false letter from a senior XXXX XXXX official in the DRC that stated that he was an employee sent to take a course in Montréal. A Canadian visitor's visa was issued on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011. The claimant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011. He spent two weeks taking the course he was registered for in Montréal.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges political problems, arrest, attack on home, false documents, and attending a course in Canada in 2011.

propositions.text: Claimant went to CIC office weeks after arrival to claim refugee protection.
propositions.quote: The claimant went to the CIC office on May 19, 2011, XXXX weeks after his arrival, to claim refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant went to CIC office weeks after arrival to claim refugee protection.

propositions.text: Panel determines claimant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection for stated reasons.
propositions.quote: The panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" for the following reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The panel determines claimant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.

propositions.text: Claimant submitted a copy of his DRC passport; original seized by CIC.
propositions.quote: To establish his identity, the claimant submitted a copy of his passport from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the original of which was seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC).1

paragraphs.summary: Claimant submitted a copy of his DRC passport; original seized by CIC.

propositions.text: Panel finds claimant's passport copy acceptable identity document under section 106 IRPA.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that this is an acceptable identity document under section 106 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds claimant's passport copy acceptable identity document under section 106 IRPA.

propositions.text: Claimant failed to credibly establish material facts supporting refugee claim; left country legally despite claiming to be wanted by ANR.
propositions.quote: The claimant failed to credibly establish the material facts alleged in support of his claim for refugee protection, namely that he left the DRC because of the facts alleged in his account. The claimant is not a trustworthy witness. He lied to the panel, deliberately concealed facts and tried to mislead the panel by submitting false documents. The claimant left his country legally even though he claimed to be wanted by the ANR.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds claimant not credible, lied, concealed facts, submitted false documents, and left country legally despite claims.

propositions.text: Claimant not credible; did not establish participation in 2010 march or arrest.
propositions.quote: The claimant is not a credible witness. He did not establish that he participated in a march in XXXX or XXXX 2010 or that he was arrested.

paragraphs.summary: Panel finds claimant not credible; did not establish participation in march or arrest.

propositions.text: Claimant stated UDPS membership and submitted 1994 UDPS card and 2013 letter confirming membership.
propositions.quote: The claimant stated that he is a member of UDPS. He submitted a UDPS card (C-4) dated 1994. The claimant established that he is a member of the party. The claimant submitted a letter dated March 25, 2013 (C-7), which states that he is regularly a registered member.

propositions.text: Claimant explained generally he fled DRC to escape dictatorial abuses and seeks safe haven.
propositions.quote: He then explained in very general terms that he fled the Democratic Republic of the Congo to escape the abuses of the existing dictatorial power and that he is seeking safe haven.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant stated UDPS membership with card and letter; explained fleeing DRC to escape dictatorship and seek safe haven.

propositions.text: Claimant testified he came to Canada for employer-requested course, planned to return, and delayed refugee claim accordingly.
propositions.quote: In his testimony, the claimant stated that he came to Canada to take a course at his employer's request. He spent two weeks taking the course in Montréal. He stated that he planned to return to the DRC, which is the reason he gave for not claiming refugee protection at the airport or within a few days of arriving.

propositions.text: UDPS letter does not mention claimant detained or wanted by ANR; only confirms membership.
propositions.quote: Nowhere in the letter does UPDS management mention that the claimant was detained or wanted by the ANR. The letter simply establishes that the claimant was a registered member of UDPS.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant testified he came for a course and planned to return; UDPS letter only confirms membership, no detention mention.

propositions.text: Claimant submitted four significant amendments to PIF and narrative without credible explanation.
propositions.quote: The claimant submitted four lists of amendments to his PIF and his narrative: June 15, 2011; May 16, 2013; July 8, 2013; and October 13, 2013. These amendments are significant, but no credible or reasonable explanation justifies them.

propositions.text: Claimant amended family member and location of ANR officer visit, showing inconsistency.
propositions.quote: The claimant made the following amendments: he added a family member to question 4. He amended the fact that the ANR officer, a friend of the family, went to see him at his sister's (amended to his cousin's). How could the claimant have mixed up his sister and his cousin when the encounter was supposed to have taken place a few days before his departure for Canada?

paragraphs.summary: Claimant made significant unexplained amendments to PIF, including family member and location inconsistencies.

propositions.text: Claimant amended month of 2010 demonstration and detention period without valid explanation.
propositions.quote: The claimant stated that he had participated in a big demonstration to protest XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX of 2010. In an amendment on June 15, 2011, the claimant changed the month of the demonstration he claimed to have attended in XXXX 2010 to XXXX and also changed the period of his detention. The claimant provided no valid explanation for why he did not remember the month in which he was allegedly arrested and detained.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant amended month of 2010 demonstration and detention period without valid explanation.

propositions.text: Panel discovered claimant applied for US visas thrice; claimant admitted lying on PIF to hide this and apologized.
propositions.quote: The claimant amended his PIF when the panel discovered, upon receiving confirmation of the fingerprints from the American authorities (produced in Exhibit A-3), that the claimant had applied for a visa for the United States three times: in 2005, 2008 and XXXX 2010. The claimant admitted to the panel that he had lied on his PIF by not declaring these facts because he did not want to jeopardize his claim for refugee protection and he apologized.

propositions.text: Not the visa applications but the claimant's untrustworthiness jeopardizes his refugee claim.
propositions.quote: It is not so much the fact that the claimant applied for an American visa three times that jeopardizes his claim for refugee protection; it is the fact that the claimant is not a witness the panel can trust.

paragraphs.summary: Panel found claimant lied about US visa applications; untrustworthiness jeopardizes claim, not visa applications themselves.

propositions.text: Claimant amended PIF about when photograph was taken; such amendments undermine credibility and raise doubts about alleged facts.
propositions.quote: The claimant also amended his Personal Information Form (PIF) to state that his photograph was taken when he was arrested in XXXX 2010 to state that the photograph was taken when he was released. Once again, it is reasonable to believe that the claimant would remember whether the photograph had been taken when he was arrested or when he was released. All these amendments to his narrative undermine his credibility and raise serious doubts about whether the claimant experienced the alleged facts.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant amended PIF about photograph timing; amendments undermine credibility and raise doubts about facts.

propositions.text: Panel entitled to draw negative inference on credibility due to major amendment or addition to PIF.
propositions.quote: According to the case law, the panel is entitled to draw a negative inference concerning credibility because of a major amendment or addition to the PIF.2

propositions.text: In this case, claimant's amendments are significant.
propositions.quote: In this case, the amendments are significant.

paragraphs.summary: Case law allows negative credibility inference from major PIF amendments; claimant's amendments are significant.

propositions.text: Photograph submitted was a posed group photo, not a mug shot; claimant tried to mislead panel by submitting it.
propositions.quote: The panel knows why the claimant amended the allegation about when the photograph was taken because, according to his narrative, he was arrested by guards who were not in uniform (line 58 and below of the narrative). However, in the photograph submitted as evidence under C-7, the soldiers are in uniform. The photograph has nothing to do with an arrest. It is a group photograph, and the people in it are posing for the photograph. If the authorities had wanted to photograph the claimant as a suspect and member of the opposition, they would have taken a [translation] "mug shot" of the claimant, that is, a close-up. It is clear that the claimant attempted to mislead the panel by submitting this photograph, which was taken under other circumstances.

propositions.text: Claimant stated he got photograph from ANR officer at sister's (amended to cousin's) home; submitting false photograph destroys credibility despite apology.
propositions.quote: The claimant stated that he got the photograph from an ANR officer who gave it to him at his sister's (amended to his cousin's) home. Submitting this false photograph as evidence destroys his credibility because, even though the claimant apologized for lying, he continued trying to mislead the panel.

paragraphs.summary: Photograph was a posed group photo, not a mug shot; claimant tried to mislead panel and destroyed credibility despite apology.

propositions.text: Claimant explained false letter obtained from NGO colleague to get into Canada; did not disclose this in narrative, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: When questioned by the panel about why he was listed in the visa application (in evidence as A-4) as being the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX when he was really a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the claimant explained that he was able to get a false XXXX letter from a colleague from another NGO in the DRC so that he could be sure of getting into Canada. The claimant did not mention this fact in his narrative but stated that he had come to participate in volunteer training for his employer. It is therefore reasonable to believe that the claimant had access to this type of service (self-ving document) through his NGO colleagues since he himself had worked in the field for over 10 years. The claimant's lack of transparency in disclosing these facts-he did so only when he had no other choice-undermines his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant obtained false letter from NGO colleague to enter Canada; nondisclosure undermines credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant tried to mislead panel by submitting false documents, destroying credibility.
propositions.quote: The claimant tried to mislead the panel by submitting false documents, which destroys his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant tried to mislead panel with false documents, destroying credibility.

propositions.text: Submitting false documents in refugee claim allows tribunal to doubt claimant's credibility.
propositions.quote: Justice Martineau states that if a claimant submits false documents to support a claim for refugee protection, it has consequences with respect to the claimant's credibility:3 [7] Producing a false document to support allegations in a refugee claim must not be minimized by the Court and legitimately allows the tribunal to doubt a claimant's credibility. (Rahaman v. Canada, 2007 FC 108, paragraphs 15 to 17).

paragraphs.summary: Case law states submitting false documents in refugee claim justifies doubting claimant's credibility.

propositions.text: The claimant is not a credible witness due to an implausible story about masked officers and his escape.
propositions.quote: The claimant is not a credible witness. He told an implausible story about how masked officers tried to arrest him in XXXX 2011.

propositions.text: The claimant's wife allegedly answered the door thinking bakers were delivering bread at 4:00 a.m.
propositions.quote: His wife allegedly answered the door because she thought that bakers were coming to deliver bread at 4:00 a.m. for their children.

propositions.text: Despite armed men besieging the house, claimant alleged he escaped by jumping out a window as soldiers did not surround the house.
propositions.quote: Even though the house was besieged by armed masked men who had come to arrest the claimant, he alleged that he was able to jump out the window because the soldiers or ANR officers had not thought to surround the house.

propositions.text: The panel observed the claimant lying and not actually experiencing the events he related.
propositions.quote: The panel was able to watch the claimant while he related these facts, and it is clear that he was lying and did not actually experience the events he was relating.

propositions.text: The panel gives no probative value to the wife's letter or the lawyer's claim due to claimant's general lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: The panel gives no probative value to the letter from his wife produced in C-6 or to the lawyer who claimed to be aware of the claimant's problems, and that is because of his general lack of credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant not credible due to an implausible story, observed lying, and disregards supporting letter and lawyer's claim.

propositions.text: Canadian refugee system relies on candour; misleading the panel affects claimant's credibility, especially if continued after apology.
propositions.quote: Justice Mainville stated that the Canadian system is based on the candour of the refugee protection claimants and that it is reasonable that misleading the panel would have consequences on the claimant's credibility, particularly if the claimant continues to do so, as is the case, even after apologizing.

propositions.text: Applicant argued adverse credibility finding was unreasonable due to contrition and reliance on 'snakehead' advice not to reveal information.
propositions.quote: The Applicant takes issue with the finding of the Panel that his credibility was tainted by the fact he lied to Canadian immigration officials by not disclosing that he had resided in the United States of America... He now asks the Canadian authorities to forgive him.

propositions.text: Judge found no merit in applicant's argument; refugee determinations require truthful declarations; failure to disclose affects credibility.
propositions.quote: I find no merit to this argument. Refugee determinations in Canada are based on voluntary and truthful declarations from claimants... His failures to declare his stay in the USA... clearly affect his credibility, and it was entirely reasonable for the Panel to draw an adverse inference from this.

paragraphs.summary: A prior court held that misleading the panel harms credibility; applicant's excuse rejected; truthful declarations are essential.

propositions.text: Claimant did not claim refugee protection immediately but waited three weeks and attended volunteer training.
propositions.quote: The panel could also talk about how the claimant did not claim refugee protection upon arriving in Canada but waited three weeks to do so. Instead, he attended volunteer training.

propositions.text: Claimant intended to return to DRC after training despite alleged gang rape of wife, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that he had intended to return to the DRC after the training despite the fact that, according to his alleged and not very credible narrative, his wife had just been gang raped because of him.

propositions.text: Claimant left with passport and Canadian visa despite claiming to be wanted by ANR, further doubting credibility.
propositions.quote: He also left with his passport and a Canadian visa even though he claimed to be wanted by the ANR, which is another valid reason to doubt his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's delayed refugee claim, intent to return despite danger, and use of passport undermine credibility.

propositions.text: Using own passport to leave country undermines credibility when claimant alleges fear of authorities.
propositions.quote: Justice Shore states that the fact that the claimant used his own passport to leave India undermined the claimant's credibility when he alleged that he was a wanted person and feared the authorities.

propositions.text: RPD reasonably concluded use of own passport showed no fear of central authorities, citing cases.
propositions.quote: The RPD reasonably concluded that the fact that Mr. Balwant Singh used his own passport to leave India demonstrated that he did not fear the central authorities.

paragraphs.summary: A prior court held that using own passport to leave undermines credibility of fear claims, supported by cited cases.

propositions.text: Claimant did not credibly establish he is a Convention refugee under section 96 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: The claimant did not credibly establish that he is a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes claimant failed to credibly establish Convention refugee status under section 96 IRPA.

propositions.text: Claimant not credible and no other evidence to support 'person in need of protection' claim; no separate section 97 analysis.
propositions.quote: The claimant was not credible and had no other evidence to support his claim of being a "person in need of protection," so the panel will not undertake a separate analysis of section 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court declines separate section 97 analysis due to claimant's lack of credibility and supporting evidence.

propositions.text: Claimant failed to prove serious possibility of persecution or risk of torture, death, or cruel treatment if returned.
propositions.quote: Having considered all the evidence, the panel determines that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or that... he would be subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to his country.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant failed to prove risk of persecution, torture, death, or cruel treatment if returned.

propositions.text: Claimant's refugee protection claim is rejected for all stated reasons.
propositions.quote: For all these reasons, XXXX XXXX XXXX claim for refugee protection is rejected.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the claimant's refugee protection claim for all stated reasons.
